title: Rural society changes

blocks.heading: Rural society changes
blocks.text: Land access, work organisation, tools, seasons and social relationships interact in rural production. Traditional practices are not timeless or uniform. Exchange, innovation and political changes can alter the resources and choices available to households.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Land use and ownership
blocks.text: Land use describes activities on land, while ownership and access arrangements describe rights and control. Community-managed access may support shared grazing; private or public arrangements have different decision structures. Identify actual rights rather than assuming communal means unrestricted.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Division of labour
blocks.text: Division of labour splits productive work into specialised tasks carried out by different workers. Household or community allocations can organise planting, herding, processing and care. Arrangements vary; do not portray gender or age roles as natural, fixed or identical everywhere.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Tools
blocks.text: Tools apply human knowledge and effort to productive tasks, from hand hoes to animal-drawn equipment. A tool’s value depends on the task, available skills, maintenance and conditions. Simple equipment can be suitable without being appropriate for every purpose.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Seasonal agriculture
blocks.text: Seasonal agriculture schedules tasks such as preparation, planting and harvesting around relevant seasonal conditions. For rain-fed crops, delayed rainfall can alter planting and labour demand. Storage and varied livelihoods can help manage a seasonal income or food gap.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Social and cultural activity
blocks.text: Shared knowledge, values and social activities can organise cooperation, mutual support and resource decisions. They can support collective work and adaptation, but members may have different interests. Consult affected people rather than assuming one speaker represents a whole community.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Local environments
blocks.text: Soil, water, vegetation and climate shape productive opportunities and constraints. Environmental knowledge can help match activities to local conditions. Dependence on rainfall or a narrow resource base can expose households to shocks without making outcomes inevitable.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Pre-colonial changes
blocks.text: Farming before colonial rule could change through local innovation, exchange of knowledge, crops and tools, and shifts in settlement and trade. Calling a system traditional does not mean it remained unchanged. Distinguish a process of adaptation from a claim that all communities adopted the same technique at one time.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Colonial influences
blocks.text: Colonial rule could reshape land control, labour obligations and market relationships, often restricting local autonomy and access. Loss of productive land or pressure to earn cash could change livelihoods and work allocation. Effects varied; explain the specific mechanism rather than treating one history as universal.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Peasant farming and cash crops
blocks.text: Smallholder or peasant farming uses household-scale productive arrangements; cash cropping grows crops primarily for sale rather than direct household consumption. A household may combine food and cash crops. Sales can finance needs, but price risk or reduced food-crop area can increase dependence on purchases.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: A seasonal constraint
blocks.text: Explain the constraint in a fictional village where planting depends on seasonal rain but workers are absent when the rain arrives. The useful planting window and available labour do not coincide. Delayed planting can limit crop establishment and expected output despite rain arriving.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect the ideas
blocks.text: Connect this lesson to Production (3.1), Sustainable Development (1.2) and Urbanisation (4.2). Identify the livelihood or resource constraint, trace the mechanism and distinguish a feasible action from a hoped-for outcome. The cases here are fictional, not claims about a named present-day community.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
